To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the motor cortex is organized into a map of the individual's motor actions rather than a map of the body, and (2) this map is used to match observed and executed actions, as well as to process action-related words and sentences.

(1) the motor cortex of monkeys and humans includes maps of coordinated movements, (2) these maps are used in the execution of movements, (3) these maps are also used for the understanding and imitation of observed movements, and (4) this neural mirroring is involved in the processing of language.

1) motor maps are organized according to actions and not body parts; 2) the organization of motor maps can be used to predict the results of studies on action observation; 3) the organization of the motor system is relevant to the embodied approach to language comprehension.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature and function of the neural mechanisms involved in the perception of action and action language comprehension, with a focus on how the motor system contributes to these processes.
the neural basis of embodied semantics and the role of the mirror neuron system in language comprehension.
how the human brain processes the motor system and how this is reflected in the language processing system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is evidence for a somatotopic map of the body in the motor cortex, which is used for motor planning and execution.

the somatotopy in action observation is a consequence of the motor system's organization and the way in which actions are encoded in the system, and not a direct reflection of the organization of the motor system itself.

the motor cortex contains a representation of body parts as well as a representation of coordinated actions, and that both representations can be used for the comprehension of action-related language.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the organization of the human motor cortex is probably based on coordinated action, not on body parts.
we have shown that the motor system is not a single, continuous representation of the body, but rather a set of representations for coordinated actions.
we have shown how a simple model of motor control can be used to account for the somatotopy found in the motor cortex and how this can be used to predict the results of neuroimaging studies.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in order to understand how the motor system is involved in the comprehension of action-related language, it is necessary to take into account the organization of motor cortex in primates, and the way this organization relates to the structure of the motor repertoire of the individual.

the motor cortex is organized in terms of the actions that the individual has learned to perform, and that these representations can be used to understand the meaning of words referring to those actions. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2019 APA, all rights reserved)
the motor system is organized to represent actions rather than body parts, and this may have important consequences for the way in which the neural substrate of embodied semantics is organized.
